lead: Every CMOS layer starts as a pattern in a polymer film called resist. Lithography prints that pattern: clean, coat, bake, align a mask, expose, develop. The resist then protects some areas while the layer below is cut away by etching or built up by deposition. Strip the resist and the wafer is ready for the next mask. The same loop runs for every layer, so its resolution sets the smallest transistor and wire. Fabs use it for all CMOS and BiCMOS products.
prereq: You need: the chapter on oxidation, diffusion and ion implantation, where thermal oxide is grown as the layer this resist patterns.

blocks.text: Lithography transfers a pattern from a mask to resist. The wafer is cleaned, coated with a light-sensitive polymer called resist, and soft baked to remove solvent. The mask (a 1× pattern) or reticle (usually 4× or 5×, reduced by the lens) is aligned to the previous layer. Light exposes the resist through the clear windows. Developer dissolves the exposed resist in a positive resist; in a negative resist the exposed part cross-links and stays, and the unexposed part dissolves. After etch or deposition, a strip removes all resist.

items: Clean and dehydrate the wafer so resist sticks.
Spin-coat resist to a uniform thickness, often below 1 μm.
Soft bake to drive off solvent.
Align the mask or reticle to the existing pattern.
Expose with UV light through the mask.
Develop: positive resist removes exposed areas; negative resist keeps them.
Etch or deposit, then strip the resist.

blocks.text: Older printers place the mask in contact with the resist (contact printing) or close to it (proximity printing). Contact printing resolves well, but mask and resist touch, so the mask picks up damage and particles. Proximity printing leaves a gap of a few to tens of micrometres, which saves the mask but blurs the image by diffraction. Projection printing uses a lens to image the reticle, so the mask never touches the wafer. Resolution is R = k·λ/NA, where R is the smallest printable feature, the half-pitch of a dense line-and-space pattern, in nm, λ is the exposure wavelength in nm, NA is the numerical aperture of the lens, and k is a process factor (about 0.5 to 0.8 for simple processes; immersion lenses and resolution-enhancement tricks bring it down to about 0.3, and 0.25 is the limit for one exposure). Depth of focus is DOF = λ/(2NA²), the vertical distance over which the image stays sharp. A shorter λ or larger NA lowers R but also lowers DOF.

blocks.where: R is the smallest printable feature (half-pitch) in nm; λ is the exposure wavelength in nm; NA is the lens numerical aperture; k is the process factor; DOF is the depth of focus in nm.

blocks.text: Etching removes material through the resist window. Wet etching uses a liquid acid or base. It is isotropic: it etches sideways at the same rate as down, so the hole undercuts the resist and ends wider than the window. Dry etching uses a plasma of ions and radicals. Reactive ion etching (RIE) combines chemical attack with ion bombardment that clears the floor of the hole, so it is anisotropic: the sidewalls stay nearly vertical. Selectivity is the etch rate of the target layer divided by the etch rate of resist or the layer below; high selectivity means the mask and underlayer survive. Endpoint detection watches the plasma emission or a reflected laser signal and stops when the target layer clears. A short over-etch, often 10-30% of the main time, removes residue.
A = 1 − (lateral etch rate / vertical etch rate)
blocks.where: A is anisotropy; A = 1 for a perfectly vertical wall, A = 0 for a fully isotropic etch.

blocks.text: Use dry etch for fine lines; wet etch for blanket removal where undercut does not matter.

Deposition adds a thin film. LPCVD (low-pressure chemical vapour deposition) runs at high temperature and gives conformal films, but the wafer sees the furnace temperature. PECVD (plasma-enhanced CVD) uses a plasma to allow lower temperatures, useful after aluminium. Sputtering strikes a target with ions and throws atoms onto the wafer; it deposits metals such as aluminium. Evaporation heats a source in vacuum; it is simple but has poor step coverage. Epitaxy grows a single-crystal silicon layer on the wafer, lattice-matched to the substrate. In BiCMOS it forms the lightly doped collector (see the chapter on BiCMOS technology).

items: LPCVD: high temperature; conformal poly-Si and nitride.
PECVD: plasma allows lower temperature; oxide and nitride over metal.
Sputtering: ion bombardment of a target; aluminium and barrier metals.
Evaporation: heated source in vacuum; simple laboratory metal films.
Epitaxy: single-crystal Si on Si; lightly doped BiCMOS collector.

blocks.text: After deposition, the surface is often not flat. CMP (chemical mechanical planarisation) polishes the wafer with a slurry and a pad until the step height falls, so the next lithography step can focus. Planarisation matters because DOF is only a few hundred nm for advanced lenses.

examples.question: A projection printer uses λ = 248 nm, NA = 0.5 and process factor k = 0.6. (a) Find the smallest printable feature R = k·λ/NA. (b) Find depth of focus DOF = λ/(2NA²). (c) Repeat both for NA = 0.6 and compare.
steps: Higher NA improves resolution (R falls from 297.6 nm to 248 nm) but reduces depth of focus (496 nm to 344 nm).
examples.answer: R = 298 nm (0.298 μm) and DOF = 496 nm at NA = 0.5; R = 248 nm and DOF = 344 nm at NA = 0.6.
examples.check:
lam = 248.0
k = 0.6
R1 = k * lam / 0.5
DOF1 = lam / (2 * 0.5**2)
R2 = k * lam / 0.6
DOF2 = lam / (2 * 0.6**2)
print(round(R1))
print(round(DOF1))
print(round(R2))
print(round(DOF2))

examples.question: A 0.5 μm oxide is etched through a 2.0 μm wide resist window. The oxide etches at 100 nm/min downward, the selectivity of oxide to resist is 5 : 1, and a 20 % over-etch is used. (a) Find the etch time. (b) Find the width of the hole at the top of the oxide for a wet etch and for RIE with anisotropy A = 0.9. (c) How much resist is lost?
steps: (a) Main etch: 500 nm ÷ 100 nm/min = 5.0 min. With 20 % over-etch: 5.0 × 1.2 = 6.0 min.
(b) Wet etch is isotropic, so the sideways rate is also 100 nm/min. Undercut per side = 100 × 6.0 = 600 nm = 0.6 μm.
Hole width at the top = 2.0 + 2 × 0.6 = 3.2 μm.
RIE: A = 1 − lateral/vertical = 0.9, so the lateral rate is 0.1 × 100 = 10 nm/min. Undercut per side = 10 × 6.0 = 60 nm.
Hole width at the top = 2.0 + 2 × 0.06 = 2.12 μm.
(c) Resist etch rate = 100 ÷ 5 = 20 nm/min, so the resist loses 20 × 6.0 = 120 nm.
examples.answer: Etch time 6.0 min; the hole is 3.2 μm wide after a wet etch but 2.12 μm after RIE; 120 nm of resist is lost.

traps: Wet etching undercuts the mask: the hole is wider than the window at the surface. A square vertical profile is wrong for wet etch.
Positive resist: the exposed part dissolves. Negative resist: the exposed part stays. Swapping them reverses the whole pattern.
A mask is 1×; a reticle is usually 4× or 5× and the projection lens reduces it. Do not use reticle dimensions directly as wafer dimensions.
R = λ/NA is incomplete; the process factor k (from about 0.8 down to 0.25) must be included. DOF is in nm, not μm, unless converted.
Over-etch is intentional, not a defect; endpoint detection is a signal, not a fixed time.

quiz.q: What is the difference between positive and negative resist?
quiz.a: Positive resist: the exposed area dissolves in developer. Negative resist: the exposed area cross-links and remains; the unexposed area dissolves.

quiz.q: Why does a larger NA improve resolution but hurt depth of focus?
quiz.a: R = kλ/NA falls as NA rises. DOF = λ/(2NA²) falls as NA² rises, so the image stays sharp over a shorter vertical range.

quiz.q: A printer has λ = 193 nm, NA = 0.7 and k = 0.5. Find R and DOF.
Why does wet etching widen a hole beyond the resist window, while RIE does not?
quiz.a: Wet etch attacks sideways as fast as down (isotropic), so it undercuts. RIE ion bombardment clears the floor and the sidewalls receive less attack, so it is anisotropic.
Selectivity is the target etch rate divided by the mask or underlayer etch rate. Endpoint detection senses when the target film clears, often by plasma emission or laser interference.

quiz.q: Why is CMP used before the next lithography step?
quiz.a: It removes step height so resist thickness is uniform and the projected image stays inside the depth of focus.

quiz.q: Why is epitaxy used for the collector in BiCMOS?
quiz.a: After the n<sup>+</sup> buried layer is implanted into the p-substrate, epitaxy grows a single-crystal, lightly doped n-type layer over it. That epi layer is the collector: light doping lets it hold the base-collector voltage. The low-resistance path under it is the buried layer, not the epi.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production lithography moved to 193 nm immersion, then EUV around 13.5 nm, and multiple patterning when one exposure cannot resolve a layer. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) now adds films one atomic layer at a time for high-k gates. Electron-beam inspection images charging and voltage contrast to find open or short defects. Search terms: EUV lithography, immersion lithography, multiple patterning, ALD, CMP dishing.
